interest: This document provides a valuable chronological index of U.S. diplomatic and military intelligence gathering on Japanese troop movements during the critical fourteen months preceding the attack on Pearl Harbor. It reveals how U.S. consular officials, military attachés, and diplomatic posts across East Asia—from Saigon and Hanoi to Canton, Dalian, Mukden, Kobe, and Tokyo—meticulously monitored the shifting dispositions of Japanese forces between the northern theater in Manchuria and the southern thrust into Southeast Asia. Of particular historiographical interest are early warnings from April 1941 concerning a planned Japanese strike on Singapore, specific intelligence on jungle-warfare training near Lang Son, and records of heavy troop departures from Kobe and Osaka coinciding with the July 1941 occupation of southern Indochina. Additionally, the docket list reflects inter-agency intelligence coordination among the State Department, War Department, Navy Department, and British allies, as well as State Department tracking of Japanese military personnel transiting the Western Hemisphere via the Panama Canal.
overview: This file consists of three consecutive sheets (Sheets 8, 9, and 10) of the U.S. State Department's 'List of Papers' (docket/purport list) for decimal file 894.23 (Internal Affairs of Japan: Movement of Japanese Troops), indexing communications numbered 100 through 133 from October 1940 to December 1941 (with one memorandum from 1942). The documents catalogued trace the strategic concentration and redeployment of the Imperial Japanese Army and Navy leading up to the Pacific War. Early entries track Japanese forces in French Indochina—including withdrawals from Kwangsi, jungle warfare training near Lang Son, troop embarkations at Haiphong, and partial withdrawals from Tonkin—as well as intelligence regarding an impending assault on Singapore. Mid-1941 entries focus on troop movements through Tientsin, the occupation of Foochow in Fukien, tight military controls and transport traffic around Canton, Sheklung, and the Pearl River, and heavy transport sailings from Kobe and Osaka. Late-summer and autumn entries document massive troop and cavalry debarkations at Dalian (Dairen) and Mukden in Manchuria, naval observations at Shanghai, the presence of Japanese military personnel in Saigon, surveillance of Japanese officers transiting the Panama Canal, and diplomatic discussions between Secretary of State Cordell Hull and Chinese Ambassador Wei Tao-Ming.

subfiles.summary: This document consists of three consecutive sheets (Sheets 8, 9, and 10) of the Department of State's List of Papers for decimal file 894.23, indexing incoming and outgoing communications concerning Japanese military movements between late 1940 and late 1941. Early entries record intelligence on Japanese troop dispositions in French Indochina, troop withdrawals from Kwangsi, transit through Tientsin, and early 1941 rumors regarding an impending attack on Singapore. Subsequent entries document naval actions and troop concentrations in South China, including the occupation of Foochow, restrictions at Sheklung, and troopship movements from Kobe and Osaka. Later entries track heavy Japanese troop debarkations and cavalry arrivals in Dalian (Dairen) and Mukden, military activities in Saigon, the transit of Japanese officers via the Panama Canal, and diplomatic discussions with Chinese Ambassador Wei Tao-Ming.
